articles.title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO

top_comments: “ In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”Feels like the most operative part of the statement.

Some takes (and from talking to nvidia people):- Delaware precedent in Caremark has a very high bar for culpability of boards in matters like this. So I suspect the combination of DoJ saying they won't prosecute combined with this standard will successfully remove their individual liability.- I'm surprised this decision was completely unanimous at the board level, considering how they quickly forced him out. Full 180 in under two weeks.- The news media is really confusing selling chips to Megaspeed then hosting them in Malaysia (giving chinese companies access - afaik still legal under the old export regime) and Megaspeed smuggling these physical chips for hosting in Chinese data centers. Former was legal and second was not.- I would not be surprised if a pardon was mentioned at some point. Will be watching how state AGs end up getting involved. CA has already subpoenaed Nvidia for this.- There was a drum circle at Nvidia from employees who were petitioning to get him backDisclosure: I co-host a podcast that talks about this. More discussion if anyone is interested: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t8nLiELIhwA

Many people here are assuming Nvidia committed some kind of crime that would've been exposed if not for government intervention. Yes the US govt is corrupt but they're likely right that there's no actual evidence. If there was, it would've already leaked from whoever's been leaking all the intelligence so far.All of the stuff coming out has been pointing the other way. CIA/AG have both said they're unsure if the woman is a spy, US politicians briefed by intelligence have all said the same. Nvidia followed normal diligence in selling GPUs to a cloud provider in Southeast Asia (including visiting their data centers), then banned Megaspeed per government request in 2025. The idea that Nvidia knew they were smuggling hasn't been suggested by anyone involved in the actual investigations. Do people think Megaspeed told Jensen they were going to smuggle chips? What would be the possible benefit of this?The Congressional committees will be about Nvidia did enough extra diligence. And there's no criminal investigation of Nvidia, only against Megaspeed, contrary to what everyone's saying.The realistic risk for Nvidia isn't that executives get hauled off to jail for arguably weak diligence, it'd be more like Seagate's export control penalty (civil fine + audit requirements). But even then Seagate's case was way more clear cut.

articles.title: "Dario is hyping the dangers so OSS models are illegal and he stays in control"
articles.summary: "Dario is hyping the dangers so OSS models are illegal and he stays in control"

top_comments: The full comment is worth reposting here in its entirety:> Dario's spiel since GPT-2 has always been about hyping the dangers so that open models would be made illegal and *he* would stay in control.> He left OpenAI because he wasn't going to have control.> It's like the Ottoman Empire banning the printing press for Arabic so they would keep in control of the dogma.> It stops the population from freely accessing diverse knowledge.> It's a new form of medieval obscurantism.Agree or disagree with LeCun, he doesn't mince words!

They're getting everybody on subsidized plans and making everybody dependent and hoping to pull the rug out and force everybody to API pricing and finally make a profit. If there's open model alternatives, they're screwed.

I work with and am friends with people who are in the regulatory space that would intersect with AI.There are some interesting conversations about how'd you ban open weight models and so far the emerging consensus is that if you can't ban the bullets, then you ban the guns. Ideas floated range from requiring companies like AMD and Nvidia to push microcode updates that limit consumer grade GPUs abilities to work with LLMs, to require some kind of registration for privately owned compute, to even just requiring that GPUs are just outright surrendered.It sounds crazy, but then I was pointed to Executed Order 6102 which is the Gold Confiscation act by FDR and opens a pathway to some kind of asset seizure. I think a lof of those in the "AI Safety-ist" camp realize that the toothpaste is out of the tube and that something that feels "draconian" in the name of state security may be needed.

top_comments: Hi, didn't expect to see this here, so adding a bit of info:They are requesting removal stating that I am using their trademarks and IP by hosting their documentation, which seems hard to work around while still keeping the site useful.People have contacted me offering to host mirrors, or suggesting I lawyer up or release the source code (sans Arm IP) to generate the same site for personal use. I'm a Kagi customer, but thoroughly uninterested in this. Fastmail is not just good enough, but good. Fastmail has been stable for decades, with a comfortable pace of progress/changes.AI is Kagi Mail's biggest selling point, but I won't ever let a cloud LLM access my emails whatsoever.

Kagi duo subscriber. Love the service and have evangelized about it to others, but worried about the feature creep and how it will affect core services. I used to love kagi translate but the quality has suffered significantly lately. And to add insult to injury, it is now capped and a separate subscription in the setting of falling quality. My s/o who used it extensively has virtually stopped due to bugs. And her search use has dropped precipitously. Before kagi, I had a proton account. I was happy with their email for years, then they added a ton of features in a short time and I was having email send and receive problems in the midst of a job hunt that reflected very poorly on my basic competence. Canceled shortly after.The point is, please don't over extend. Response time for support tickets is already in months.

Not sure I like it. What bugs me is that Kagi - in my perception - ran on the idea they don't really store user data (no search history, assistant conversations expire by default, all that's persisted there is basic user account data), and this seem to be a major paradigm change. While I trust them to not pull any switcheroos and not abuse this, that's still a notable change that may affect how Kagi sees themselves.Plus, if you don't have the data you can't be even tempted to do anything its owners wouldn't enjoy. If you do have the data...Either way, while I'm a very happy Kagi Search user, I self-host my mail, so I'm not a target audience for this product.

articles.title: Stalwart is now a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange
articles.summary: Stalwart is now a drop-in replacement for Microsoft Exchange

top_comments: The only issue is regulatory: As a freelancer or company in Germany, you have to archive mail in a way that can’t be deleted or altered and store it for access by the tax authorities for up to 10 years (“GoBD”). Stalwart does not have this feature in their regular plans (or the OSS variants)
Stalwart is the mail server Mozilla’s Thundermail uses.

The lock-in effect is inherent to the protocol and the clients. Furthermore, supporting MAPI and similar standards merely buys time and saves on licensing costs when your target is OSS.While I recognize the practical benefit for an administrator, in my view, anything that expands the protocol stack surrounding Microsoft email ultimately does a disservice to the remainder of the still-existing, open email ecosystem.
